title: Debt Securities

brief.md:
- A **bond** = a **loan** from the investor to the issuer (corporation, government or municipality). Bondholders are **creditors**, not owners, and rank **ahead of shareholders** in bankruptcy or liquidation.
- Bonds and other securities paying a regular income stream are **fixed-income securities**. Issuers use bonds as an alternative to stock for raising capital (**debt financing**).
- The investor is promised the **principal** back plus **interest**.

| Form | Who holds the record | Interest | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Bearer** | **Nobody** — issuer keeps no record | Clip **coupon**, present to a paying agent (typically any bank) | Not issued since **1983**; a few still trade; seller makes **physical delivery** |
| **Fully registered** | Owner’s name recorded with **issuer or transfer agent** | Sent **automatically** to the owner; no coupons | Certificate may exist, but it has no coupons |
| **Book-entry** | Recorded **electronically by a central depository** | Automatic | **Most common** method today; no physical transfer |

- Registered and book-entry bonds are protected from **loss or theft** and pay principal and interest automatically.
- Difference between registered and book-entry: **who keeps the records** (issuer/transfer agent vs central depository).
> **Exam tip** Bearer = whoever holds it gets paid. Book-entry = most common. Any “benefit of registered/book-entry” answer never includes physical coupons.

brief.h: Par value, quotes and price conversion
brief.md:
- **Par value** (face value, principal) = amount repaid at **maturity**; normally **$1,000**. A new issue usually sells **close to par**.
- Aggregate par of an issue = total dollars raised (e.g. $10 million of bonds).
- **Market price** is what investors pay in secondary trading and **fluctuates**, mainly with **interest rates**. It is not the same as par.
- Quotes are a **percentage of par** on a point scale: **100 = par = $1,000**.

| Quote | Meaning | Price |
|---|---|---|
| Above 100 | **Premium** | e.g. 105 → **$1,050** |
| 100 | **Par** | $1,000 |
| Below 100 | **Discount** | e.g. 95 → **$950** |

- Conversion for a $1,000 bond: **quote × 10**. Quote 97 → $970; 112 → $1,120.
- Fractions: **1/8ths** for corporate and municipal bonds, **1/32nds** for government bonds. Convert fraction → decimal, add to the whole number, multiply by 10 (98 1/8 → 98.125 → **$981.25**).
- Bonds can also be quoted by **yield to maturity**: annualised return if held to maturity.
> **Exam tip** Always assume **$1,000 par** unless the question says otherwise.

brief.h: Coupon, interest payment dates and special structures
brief.md:
- **Coupon** = interest paid to the bondholder, expressed as a % of **par**. The coupon rate is the **nominal yield (NY)**.
- Most bonds pay **semiannually** (two equal installments). A 10% coupon = $100 a year = **$50 every six months**.
- Interest is always computed on **par**, **never** on the price paid.
- Payment-date codes: **J&J, F&A, M&S, A&O, M&N, J&D**. Paid on the **1st** of the month unless “**15**” follows (J&J 15 → Jan 15 and Jul 15).
- **At maturity** the investor receives **par + the final semiannual coupon** (3-year 5% bond bought at 86: final cash = $25 + $1,000 = **$1,025**).
- **Fixed-rate**: coupon never changes. **Floating / adjustable / variable-rate**: coupon resets with a **benchmark** (e.g. Treasury bill rate).
- **Zero-coupon bonds**: no periodic interest; bought at a **deep discount**, redeemed at par; the difference is the interest. Usually **10+ years**, so suited to long-range goals (retirement, college). **Prices swing more** than other bonds. Investors are taxed each year on **imputed (phantom) interest** even though nothing is received until maturity.
- **Term bonds**: whole issue matures on **one date**. **Serial bonds**: a portion matures **each year**.
> **Exam tip** Zero-coupon bonds do pay interest — just **all at maturity**. They have **no reinvestment risk** and the only meaningful yield is **YTM**.

brief.h: Price vs interest rates, basis points, maturity
brief.md:
- Interest rates and bond prices move in **opposite directions**: rates up → prices of outstanding bonds **down**; rates down → prices **up**. Rates are the **primary driver** of price (more than rating, demand or earnings).
- Why: with new bonds at 6%, an old 5% bond must fall in price to compete; with new bonds at 3.5%, an old 5% bond trades at a **premium**.
- Applies to all fixed-rate investments, including **preferred stock** (regular dividend, trades like a bond).
- Market value above par = **premium**; below par = **discount**.
- **Basis point** = 0.01%; **100 bps = 1%**. A yield move from 0.75% to 0.85% = **10 bps**. Calculator: 50 bps → 0.005.
- **Maturity** is set at issue, from as short as **one day** to as long as **30 years**. Longer maturity → **higher coupon** demanded and **greater price swings**.
- **Pull to par**: a discount bond’s price **rises** toward par, a premium bond’s price **falls** toward par as maturity nears.
> **Exam tip** Long maturity + low coupon (zero is the extreme) = most price volatility. Duration measures this; calculation not tested, **longer duration = more rate-sensitive**.

brief.h: Call, put and sinking fund provisions
brief.md:
- **Callable bond**: the **issuer** may redeem before maturity. Must be disclosed **at issue** with call dates and prices. Interest **stops** when the bond is called.
- **Call premium** = amount above par paid for early redemption; usually **higher the earlier** the call (e.g. $1,050 in year 5, $1,025 in year 10).
- **Refunding**: issuer calls bonds when **rates fall** and sells cheaper new bonds, like a homeowner refinancing (6% bonds replaced at 4% saves 2% a year).
- If called, the holder gets **par + final semiannual coupon + call premium (if any)**. Example: $1,000 par, 6%, callable at 102 → $1,000 + $30 + $20 = **$1,050**.
- Callable bonds are **riskier for investors**, so they pay a **higher rate** than non-callable. The call feature benefits the **issuer only**.
- **Call protection** = period after issue when the bond cannot be called. A bond callable after year 10 can be called **any time from year 10 to maturity**.
- Most corporate and municipal bonds with maturities over **10 years** are callable; **federal government bonds are not callable**.
- **Puttable bond**: the **investor** may demand early repayment on a trigger (rating downgrade, rates above a set level) on dates set in the contract. Benefits investors, so it pays **less interest** than a straight bond.
- **Sinking fund**: issuer regularly sets money aside in an **escrow account** held by a third party (typically a bank) to retire bonds. Enhances **safety and liquidity** and ensures funds are available.
> **Exam tip** Call = issuer’s option, higher yield for investor. Put = investor’s option, lower yield. Issuer calls when rates are **declining**.

brief.h: Yields: NY, CY, YTM, YTC and the yield ladder
brief.md:
| Yield | What it measures | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Nominal (NY)** | Coupon ÷ par | **Fixed for life**; equals the coupon |
| **Current (CY)** | **Annual interest ÷ current market price** | Ignores gain or loss at maturity; **semiannual coupon × 2** first |
| **Yield to maturity (YTM)** | Total return if held to maturity | **Most widely quoted**; uses price, par, coupon, time; assumes coupons reinvested at the YTM; **calculation not tested** |
| **Yield to call (YTC)** | Return if called at the **first** call date | Like YTM but uses years to call and includes the call premium |

- YTM wording: “trading on a 9.5 basis”, “trading at 9.5%”, “yielding 9.5%”.
- CY and price move **inversely**: a falling price raises CY.

| Bond trades at | Yield ladder |
|---|---|
| **Premium** | **NY > CY > YTM > YTC** (YTC lowest) |
| **Discount** | **NY < CY < YTM < YTC** (NY lowest) |
| **Par** | NY = CY = YTM = YTC |

- Premium: YTC below YTM because the premium is lost faster. Discount: YTC above YTM because the discount is recovered faster.
- If **YTM > coupon** → bought at a **discount**. If **YTM < coupon** → **premium**. 5% bond yielding 5.5% = discount; 7% bond yielding 6.2% = premium.
> **Exam tip** Zero-coupon: numerator is zero, so NY and CY are not meaningful; **YTM** is the yield that counts. For YTC with several call dates, use the **first**.

| Risk | Definition | Key facts |
|---|---|---|
| **Interest rate** | Value changes as rates change | Rates up → prices down. **Largest effect on price.** Greater for **longer maturity** and **lower/zero coupon** |
| **Call** | Issuer redeems when rates fall | Investor loses the high coupon; non-callable bonds give **call protection** |
| **Reinvestment** | Cannot find a similar return after a call or when reinvesting coupons | Falling rates hurt; **zero-coupon bonds have none** (no coupon to reinvest) |
| **Inflation / purchasing power** | Fixed payments buy less over time | Hits **bonds and preferred stock**; measured by **CPI**; deflation helps fixed income |
| **Credit / default** | Issuer fails to pay interest or principal | A **missed interest payment = default**; lower credit quality → higher yield |

- Floating-rate bonds have little or no interest rate risk; a **held-to-maturity zero** has no interest rate risk on principal, but its **price** still swings before then.
- High inflation can push the Fed to **raise rates**, which lowers bond prices (a second hit to bondholders).
- **US government** securities are risk-free from a **credit** perspective (government can tax) but still have **interest rate and inflation risk**.
> **Exam tip** Rank for interest rate risk: **30-year zero** is the worst; 1-year high-coupon the best. Call risk causes reinvestment risk.

- **Rating agencies** (S&P, Moody’s, Fitch) publish credit quality. Higher rating → lower default chance → **lower yield**. Lower rating → higher yield.

| Category | S&P / Fitch | Moody’s |
|---|---|---|
| Highest | **AAA** | **Aaa** |
| Investment grade (lowest is BBB−) | AA, A, **BBB** | Aa, A, **Baa** (lowest Baa3) |
| Non-investment grade (junk / high yield) | **BB+** and below, down to CCC, CC, C, D | **Ba1** and below, down to Caa, Ca, C |

- Non-investment-grade = **junk** or **high-yield** bonds: more credit risk, higher yield.
- Government bonds (especially US federal) have the **lowest default risk and lowest returns**; corporates carry more credit risk and pay more.
- A rating **can change while the bond is outstanding**.
- **EMMA** (Electronic Municipal Market Access) is a **public website run by the MSRB** for researching and tracking municipal bonds: issuers, bond descriptions, pricing, interest rates, credit ratings.
> **Exam tip** Lowest investment grade: **BBB (S&P) / Baa (Moody’s)**. One notch lower (BB / Ba) is junk.

- If a bond is sold **between coupon dates**, the seller has earned part of the coming coupon. The **buyer pays accrued interest to the seller**, added to the price. The bond trades **“and interest”** (with interest).
- Day count:

| Bond type | Year / month basis |
|---|---|
| **Corporate, municipal, agency** | **360-day year, 30-day months** |
| **Treasury notes and bonds** | **365-day year, actual days per month** |

- **Regular-way settlement is T+1** (corporate, municipal, Treasury). **Cash settlement = same day** as trade.
- Count days **from the last coupon date (included) up to the settlement date (excluded)**.
- **Formula**: rate × par × days ÷ 360 (or 365 for Treasuries).
- **New issues** with no prior coupon: count from the **dated date**; the first payment may cover an **irregular period** longer or shorter than six months.
- **Trade flat** (no accrued interest): bonds **in default** and **zero-coupon** bonds.
- Tax: accrued interest received is **ordinary interest income** and does **not** change the bond’s **cost basis**. It appears on **both** confirmations.
> **Exam tip** Settlement day is excluded from the count. Corporate example: 4% bond, last coupon Dec 1, trade Apr 9, settlement Apr 10 → 129 days → $14.33.

- The IRS requires investors to move the **cost basis** toward par each year; cost basis drives the taxable gain or loss on a sale before maturity.
- **Accretion** (bought at a **discount**): basis adjusted **up** toward par. **Amortization** (bought at a **premium**): basis adjusted **down** toward par.
- Both use **straight-line**: |par − price| ÷ years to maturity = yearly adjustment. At maturity, basis = **$1,000**.
- Examples: $900 bond, 10 years → $10 a year; basis $910 after year one. $1,100 bond, 5 years → $20 a year; basis $1,080 after year one.
> **Exam tip** Discount → **Accrete** (adds up). Premium → **Amortize** (subtracts). Accrued interest never touches basis; accretion and amortization do.

traps: **Coupon vs market price.** Interest is computed on **par**, not on what the investor paid. A 5% bond bought at 86 still pays $25 every six months.
**Nominal vs current yield.** NY = coupon ÷ **par** and never changes. CY = annual interest ÷ **current price** and moves **inversely** with price.
**Semiannual coupon in the CY formula.** If the question gives a $25 semiannual payment, annual interest is **$50**. Forgetting to double it halves the answer.
**Premium vs discount ladder.** Premium: NY highest, YTC lowest. Discount: NY lowest, YTC highest. At par all four are equal.
**YTM above or below the coupon.** YTM greater than coupon = **discount**; YTM lower than coupon = **premium**. Do not reverse it.
**Call vs put.** Call = **issuer’s** right (investor demands a higher rate). Put = **investor’s** right (investor accepts a lower rate).
**When the issuer calls.** Issuers call when rates are **falling** (refunding). Rising rates make the old low coupon attractive, so no call.
**Call proceeds.** Holder receives **par + final coupon + premium**, then interest stops. Quoting only par or only par plus premium is wrong.
**Callable after 10 years.** Means any time from year 10 **through maturity**, not only in year 10. Call protection is the period before.
**Accrued interest day count.** Include the **last coupon date**, exclude the **settlement date**. Corporate/muni/agency use **30/360**; Treasuries use **actual/365**.
**Trade date vs settlement date.** Regular way is **T+1**; accrued interest runs to settlement, not to the trade date. Cash settlement is same day.
**Zero-coupon bonds.** They do pay interest, all at maturity, yet are **taxed annually** on phantom interest. They have **no reinvestment risk** but the **highest interest rate risk**.
**Accretion vs amortization.** Accretion = discount bond, basis rises. Amortization = premium bond, basis falls. Both straight-line to par; accrued interest does not affect basis.
**Lowest investment grade.** BBB (S&P) or Baa (Moody’s). BB or Ba is junk. A rating can change while the bond is outstanding.

formulas.name: Quote to dollar price
formulas.rule: Price = quote × 10 for a $1,000 par bond.  Fractions: convert to decimal (1/8 = 0.125; use the same method for 32nds), add to the whole number, then × 10.  Above 100 = premium; below 100 = discount.

formulas.name: Current yield (CY)
formulas.rule: CY = Annual interest ÷ Current market price.  Semiannual coupon → multiply by 2 first.  Price ↓ → CY ↑.  Discount: CY > NY.  Premium: CY < NY.

formulas.name: Yield ladder and decision rule
formulas.rule: Premium: NY > CY > YTM > YTC.  Discount: NY < CY < YTM < YTC.  Par: all equal.  YTM > coupon → discount; YTM < coupon → premium.  YTC uses the first call date and the call premium.
formulas.example: A 4% bond yielding 4.6% to maturity: YTM above coupon → **discount**, so CY is above 4% and below 4.6%, YTC is above 4.6%.

formulas.name: Accrued interest
formulas.rule: Accrued = Rate × Par × Days ÷ Basis.  Corporate/muni/agency: 30/360.  Treasury notes and bonds: actual days / 365.  Count from last coupon date (included) to settlement date (excluded).  Regular way = T+1.
formulas.example: 5% corporate bond, coupons Jan 1 / Jul 1, trade Mon Mar 14 → settles Tue Mar 15. Days: Jan 30 + Feb 30 + Mar 14 = 74. $50 × 74 ÷ 360 = **$10.28**.

formulas.name: Accretion and amortization (straight-line)
formulas.rule: Yearly adjustment = |Par − Purchase price| ÷ Years to maturity.  Discount → accrete (basis up).  Premium → amortize (basis down).  Basis = $1,000 at maturity.
formulas.example: Bought at $940 with 6 years left: $60 ÷ 6 = $10 a year; basis after year 2 = **$960**. Bought at $1,060 with 4 years: $60 ÷ 4 = $15; basis after year 1 = **$1,045**.

formulas.name: Cash received at maturity, on call, and basis-point moves
formulas.rule: Maturity: par + final semiannual coupon.  Call: par + final semiannual coupon + call premium (stops interest).  100 bps = 1%; 1 bp = 0.01% = 0.0001.

glossary.d: A security issued by a corporation or governmental entity to raise capital; a loan from the investor in return for interest and principal.
A bond or other security paying a regular stream of income to the investor.
Raising money by borrowing from investors (bonds) rather than selling ownership.
A bond with physical certificate and coupons where the issuer keeps no ownership record; payment goes to whoever holds it; no longer issued.
A bond whose owner’s name is recorded with the issuer or transfer agent, with interest paid automatically and no coupons.
Electronic recording of ownership by a central depository; the most common way bond ownership is tracked.
The face amount repaid at maturity, normally $1,000 per bond.
The price at which a bond trades, expressed as a percentage of par on a point scale (100 = par).
A bond trading above par (quote above 100).
A bond trading below par (quote below 100).
The interest paid to the bondholder, stated as a percentage of par.
The coupon rate; interest divided by par; fixed for the life of the bond.
A bond whose coupon resets with a benchmark such as the Treasury bill rate; also called adjustable- or variable-rate.
A bond paying no periodic interest, sold at a deep discount and redeemed at par; the difference is the interest.
Interest on a zero-coupon bond that accrues and is taxable each year though it is not received until maturity.
One one-hundredth of a percentage point (0.01%); 100 bps equals 1%.
The date on which principal is returned to bondholders; from one day to 30 years.
An issue in which all bonds mature on a single date.
An issue in which a portion of the bonds matures each year.
Money the issuer regularly sets aside in escrow with a third party to retire bonds, enhancing safety and liquidity.
A bond the issuer has the right to redeem before maturity at a stated price.
The amount above par paid to investors when a bond is called early.
A period after issue during which a bond cannot be called.
Calling outstanding bonds and selling cheaper new ones when interest rates have declined.
A bond giving the investor the right to demand early repayment of principal on a specified event or date.
Annual interest divided by the current market price of the bond.
The most widely quoted yield, including the gain or loss from price to par if held to maturity.
The return if the bond is called on the first possible call date, including any call premium.
The risk that bond prices fall as interest rates rise.
A measure of a bond’s sensitivity to interest rate changes; longer duration means more sensitivity.
The risk that the issuer redeems a bond when rates fall, causing the investor to lose a high coupon.
The risk that proceeds or coupons must be reinvested at a lower rate than the bond was paying.
The risk that fixed returns buy less over time because prices rise, measured by the CPI.
The measure of the average price change of consumer goods and services purchased by households.
The risk that the issuer cannot pay interest or repay principal.
A bond rated BBB/Baa3 or higher, with lower default risk and lower yield.
A non-investment-grade bond with higher default risk and a higher yield.
Electronic Municipal Market Access, the public MSRB website for researching municipal bonds.
Interest earned since the last coupon date, paid by the buyer to the seller on top of the price.
The date from which interest begins to accrue on a new issue.
Trading without accrued interest, as with bonds in default and zero-coupon bonds.
The value of an asset for tax purposes, used to calculate capital gain or loss.
Straight-line upward adjustment of cost basis on a discount bond toward par.
Straight-line downward adjustment of cost basis on a premium bond toward par.

cards.f: What is a bond, legally and economically?
cards.b: A **loan** from investor to issuer. Bondholders are **creditors**, ranking ahead of shareholders in bankruptcy.

cards.f: Bearer bond: how is interest collected?
cards.b: **Clip the coupon** and present it to a paying agent (typically any bank). The issuer keeps **no ownership record**.

cards.f: When did bearer bond issuance stop, and how do the few survivors trade?
cards.b: Not issued since **1983**; a few trade in the secondary market with **physical delivery** of the certificate.

cards.f: Fully registered bond: who has the ownership record?
cards.b: The **issuer or a transfer agent**. Interest is sent automatically; no coupons on the certificate.

cards.f: Book-entry: who keeps the record, and how common is it?
cards.b: A **central depository**, electronically. It is the **most common** method today.

cards.f: Default par value to assume on the exam?
cards.b: **$1,000** per bond unless the question says otherwise.

cards.f: Bond quoted at 104. Price, and premium or discount?
cards.b: 104 × 10 = **$1,040**; trades at a **premium**.

cards.f: Which fractions are used in corporate/municipal quotes versus government quotes?
cards.b: Corporate and municipal: **1/8ths**. Government: **1/32nds**.

cards.f: Convert a quote of 102 1/4 to dollars.
Nominal yield is another name for what?
cards.b: The **coupon rate**, expressed as a percentage of **par**.

cards.f: What does J&D 15 mean?
cards.b: Interest paid on **June 15 and December 15**. Without “15”, payment is on the 1st.

cards.f: What does an investor receive on the maturity date of a 4% bond?
cards.b: **Par ($1,000) plus the final semiannual coupon ($20)** = $1,020.

cards.f: Is coupon interest based on par or the purchase price?
cards.b: **Par.** Buying at a discount or premium does not change the dollar coupon.

cards.f: Floating-rate bond: what drives the coupon?
cards.b: A **benchmark** (e.g. Treasury bill rate); the coupon rises and falls with it.

cards.f: Zero-coupon bond: where does the investor’s return come from?
cards.b: Buying at a **deep discount** and receiving **par at maturity**. The difference is the interest.

cards.f: Typical maturity of a zero-coupon bond and why that suits goals like college funding?
cards.b: Usually **10+ years**; interim coupons don’t matter for a long-range goal.

cards.f: Tax on zero-coupon bonds before maturity?
cards.b: Investors owe tax each year on **imputed (phantom) interest** even though no cash is received.

cards.f: What happens to existing bond prices when market rates rise?
cards.b: They **fall**: new bonds pay more, so old lower-coupon bonds must be cheaper.

cards.f: Rates fall to 3.5% and your bond pays 5%. What happens to its price?
cards.b: It **rises**, trading at a **premium**, since investors pay up for the higher coupon.

cards.f: Which non-bond security also trades inversely to rates?
cards.b: **Preferred stock**: its regular dividend makes it trade like a bond.

cards.f: Define basis point and give the conversion.
A yield goes from 4.53% to 4.73%. How many basis points?
Why do long-term bonds usually pay more interest than short-term?
cards.b: Greater **uncertainty** over a longer period; they also swing more in price.

cards.f: Bond bought at 93 approaches maturity. Which way does the price move?
cards.b: **Up toward par** ($1,000); a premium bond drifts down toward par.

cards.f: What is a sinking fund and where is the money held?
cards.b: Regular issuer set-asides to retire bonds, held in **escrow with a third party** (typically a bank); boosts safety and liquidity.

cards.f: Who benefits from a call feature?
cards.b: The **issuer** only. Investors lose the high coupon, so callable bonds pay a **higher rate**.

cards.f: What is the call premium and how does it change with time?
cards.b: Amount **above par** paid on early redemption; **higher the earlier** the call.

cards.f: When do issuers call bonds?
cards.b: When interest rates are **declining**: they refund with cheaper new debt.

cards.f: Define refunding.
cards.b: Calling outstanding bonds and issuing **cheaper new bonds** after rates fall, like a mortgage refinance.

cards.f: 6% bond callable at 102, called. What does the holder receive?
cards.b: $1,000 par + $30 final coupon + $20 premium = **$1,050**; interest then stops.

cards.f: 20-year bond callable after year 10: when can it be called?
cards.b: **Any time from year 10 through maturity**, not only in year 10.

cards.f: Put feature: who holds the option and what triggers it?
cards.b: The **investor**; e.g. a rating downgrade or rates rising above a set level, on dates in the contract.

cards.f: Current yield formula and the semiannual trap.
cards.b: **Annual interest ÷ market price.** A semiannual coupon must be **multiplied by 2**.

cards.f: 5% bond ($50 a year) trades at 125. Current yield?
Bond price falls; what happens to current yield?
cards.b: It **rises**, because price is the denominator.

cards.f: Which yield is most widely quoted and will you calculate it on the exam?
cards.b: **Yield to maturity**; it needs a financial calculator and is **not** calculated on the exam.

cards.f: Which call date is used for yield to call?
cards.b: The **first** possible call date, plus any call premium on it.

cards.f: Premium bond: order of NY, CY, YTM, YTC.
cards.b: **NY > CY > YTM > YTC**; YTC is lowest.

cards.f: Discount bond: order of the four yields.
cards.b: **NY < CY < YTM < YTC**; NY is lowest.

cards.f: A 6% bond yields 6.8% to maturity. Premium, par or discount?
cards.b: **Discount**: YTM above the coupon.

cards.f: What affects bond prices most?
cards.b: **Changing interest rates**, more than credit rating, demand or earnings.

cards.f: Which bonds have the greatest interest rate risk?
cards.b: **Longer maturity** and **lower or zero coupon**; longer duration = more rate-sensitive.

cards.f: Define call risk.
cards.b: The issuer redeems the bond when rates fall, so the investor **loses the relatively high coupon**.

cards.f: Define reinvestment rate risk and the bond type immune to it.
cards.b: Risk of reinvesting proceeds or coupons at a **lower rate**. **Zero-coupon bonds** have none: no coupon to reinvest.

cards.f: What is inflationary risk, and which index measures inflation?
cards.b: Fixed payments lose **purchasing power**; measured by the **CPI**.

cards.f: How does high inflation hurt bond prices through the Fed?
cards.b: The Fed may **raise rates** to curb inflation, which **lowers bond prices**.

cards.f: Why are US government securities called risk-free for credit?
cards.b: The government can raise money through **taxation**; they still have interest rate and inflation risk.

cards.f: Lowest investment-grade ratings at S&P and Moody’s?
cards.b: S&P **BBB**; Moody’s **Baa**. Below that is non-investment grade (junk).

cards.f: What is EMMA and who runs it?
cards.b: Electronic Municipal Market Access: a **public website run by the MSRB** for municipal bond research.

cards.f: Who pays accrued interest in a trade and to whom?
cards.b: The **buyer pays the seller**, on top of the price.

cards.f: Day-count basis for corporate, municipal and agency bonds.
cards.b: **360-day year, 30-day months.**

cards.f: Day-count basis for Treasury notes and bonds.
cards.b: **365-day year, actual days.**

cards.f: Regular-way settlement for corporate, municipal and Treasury bonds?
cards.b: **T+1**: one business day after trade date. Cash settlement is same day.

cards.f: Which dates are included in the accrued interest day count?
cards.b: Include the **last coupon date**; stop **before the settlement date**.

cards.f: Which bonds trade flat?
cards.b: Bonds **in default** and **zero-coupon** bonds: no accrued interest.

cards.f: Accretion versus amortization.
cards.b: Accretion: **discount** bond, basis **up** to par. Amortization: **premium** bond, basis **down** to par. Both straight-line.

cards.f: Bond bought at $920 with 8 years left. Annual accretion and basis after year 3?

questions.q: Which form of bond ownership leaves the issuer with no record of who owns the bond?
w: Correct: the issuer keeps no ownership record, so whoever physically holds the certificate and coupons is paid.
Wrong: the owner’s name is recorded with the issuer or its transfer agent, so a record clearly exists.
Wrong: a central depository records ownership electronically, so ownership is fully documented.
Wrong: the transfer agent is simply the party keeping the owner’s name on record, which is the opposite of no record.

questions.q: All of the following are benefits of holding bonds in registered or book-entry form EXCEPT:
o: protection against lost or stolen certificates
automatic payment of interest and principal
physical coupons that the holder must clip
w: Wrong: this is a genuine benefit because ownership is recorded and cannot be lost with a piece of paper.
Wrong: this is a genuine benefit since the owner never has to present anything to be paid.
Correct: this is the feature of bearer bonds, not registered or book-entry, so it is not a benefit of these forms.
Wrong: this is a real benefit of book-entry, where a depository simply changes its records.

questions.q: What is the main difference between a fully registered bond and a book-entry bond?
o: Registered bonds pay interest by coupon; book-entry bonds do not
Book-entry ownership is recorded by a central depository rather than the issuer or transfer agent
Book-entry bonds are payable to whoever holds the certificate
Registered bonds cannot be sold in the secondary market
w: Wrong: neither form uses coupons, so interest delivery is not the distinguishing feature.
Correct: the difference is who keeps the ownership records, which is the depository for book-entry bonds.
Wrong: that describes a bearer bond; book-entry has no certificate at all.
Wrong: registered bonds trade freely in the secondary market; only the ownership record held by the issuer or agent is updated.

questions.q: A corporate bond is quoted at 108 3/8. Assuming $1,000 par, what is the dollar price of one bond, ignoring accrued interest?
w: Correct: 3/8 = 0.375, so 108.375 × 10 = $1,083.75 (convert the fraction, add to the whole number, multiply by 10).
Wrong: this treats the fraction as 0.038 rather than 0.375, which misconverts the eighths.
Wrong: this swaps digits; 108.375 multiplied by 10 is $1,083.75, not $1,038.75.
Wrong: this adds an extra 25 points; the quote is 108 and three-eighths, which is $1,083.75.

questions.q: An investor buys five bonds quoted at 96. Ignoring accrued interest and commissions, what is the total principal cost?
w: Wrong: this divides by ten instead of multiplying; a quote of 96 means 96% of par.
Correct: each bond costs 96 × 10 = $960, and 5 × $960 = $4,800.
Wrong: this adds the quote to par; the bonds are at a discount, so the cost is below $5,000.
Wrong: this assumes $992 per bond; a quote of 96 is $960 per bond, so five cost $4,800.

questions.q: A bond carries an 8% coupon and is marked J&J 15. How much interest does the holder of one $1,000 bond receive and when?
w: Wrong: the 15 after the months moves payment to the 15th, so the 1st-of-month dates are wrong.
Wrong: a bond paying 8% pays $80 a year but in two semiannual installments, not once.
Correct: 8% × $1,000 = $80 a year, split into two $40 payments on the 15th of the months shown.
Wrong: $80 is the annual total; each semiannual installment is half that, or $40.

questions.q: Mira buys a three-year bond with a 6% coupon at a price of 92 and holds it to maturity. What is her total cash payment on the maturity date?
w: Correct: at maturity she gets par $1,000 plus the final semiannual coupon of $30 (6% × $1,000 ÷ 2).
Wrong: this adds a full year of coupons; only the final semiannual payment of $30 comes with par.
Wrong: this omits the final semiannual coupon, which is paid on top of par at maturity.
Wrong: this adds the coupon to her purchase price of $920; the redemption is based on par, not the price paid.

questions.q: All of the following are true of zero-coupon bonds EXCEPT:
o: they are sold at a deep discount to par
the owner may owe annual tax on imputed interest
they pay semiannual interest on the first of the month
w: Wrong: this is true; the discount is how the investor earns the return.
Wrong: this is true; phantom interest accrues each year and is generally taxable.
Wrong: this is true; with no coupons paid there is nothing to reinvest.
Correct: this is false because a zero-coupon bond pays no periodic interest and all of the return arrives at maturity.

questions.q:
A parent buys a 15-year zero-coupon bond at $620 to fund college. Which of the following are TRUE?
I. The return is realized as the difference between $620 and par at maturity
II. Tax may be owed each year on interest that accrues
III. The parent receives semiannual interest checks
IV. There is no reinvestment risk on coupons
w: Wrong: statement III is false because zero-coupon bonds pay no semiannual interest, and IV is also true.
Correct: I, II and IV are all true: return comes at maturity, phantom interest is taxed yearly, and no coupons exist to reinvest.
Wrong: this includes III, which is false, and leaves out the true statement I.
Wrong: statement III is false, so not every statement can be selected.

questions.q: A bond was issued with a 5% coupon. Today newly issued comparable bonds carry 6.5%. The 5% bond most likely trades:
w: Wrong: a premium would require market rates to be below 5%, but they are higher.
Correct: buyers can get 6.5% on new bonds, so the 5% bond must be priced below par to compete.
Wrong: par would mean the coupon matches market rates, which it does not.
Wrong: the call price is set in the offering documents and is unrelated to how rates move the market price.

questions.q:
An investor owns a 4.5% bond. Comparable new bonds are now issued at 3%. Which of the following are TRUE of the investor’s bond?
I. Its market price has risen
II. It trades at a premium
III. Its current yield is higher than its nominal yield
IV. Its current yield is lower than its nominal yield
w: Wrong: III is false: a rising price lowers current yield below nominal yield, not above it.
Wrong: this misses that the price rose and includes the false statement III.
Correct: falling rates push the price up, the bond trades above par, and current yield falls below the 4.5% nominal yield.
Wrong: III is false for a premium bond; the current yield is below the nominal yield.

questions.q: A bond’s yield was 3.85% in the morning and rose 15 basis points during the day. What was the closing yield?
w: Correct: 15 bps equals 0.15%, so a starting yield of 3.85% plus 0.15% gives a closing yield of 4.00%.
Wrong: this subtracts the move from the opening yield, but the question says the yield rose during the day.
Wrong: this adds 1.5 percentage points, confusing 15 bps with 150 bps.
Wrong: this treats 15 bps as 0.015%; one basis point is 0.01%, so 15 bps is 0.15%.

questions.q: One bond trades at 94 and another at 108, each with eight years to maturity. All else equal, what happens to their prices as maturity nears?
o: The 94 bond rises toward par and the 108 bond falls toward par
w: Wrong: only the discount bond rises; a premium bond must fall toward par.
Correct: prices converge on par at maturity, so the discount bond climbs and the premium bond declines.
Wrong: only the premium bond falls toward par; the discount bond moves up toward par as maturity nears.
Wrong: prices drift toward par as maturity approaches rather than staying fixed.

questions.q: Which statement about a sinking fund provision is TRUE?
o: It gives bondholders protection from the issuer’s call
It protects the bond’s price from rising interest rates
The issuer sets money aside in an escrow account held by a third party to help retire the bonds
It raises the coupon paid to investors
w: Wrong: a sinking fund is about setting aside money, not about restricting calls.
Wrong: a sinking fund does not change how sensitive the bond’s price is to moves in market interest rates.
Correct: regular set-asides in escrow improve the safety and liquidity of the issue.
Wrong: a sinking fund adds safety, which if anything lowers the required yield.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes refunding?
o: An issuer calls outstanding bonds and sells cheaper new bonds after interest rates have fallen
An investor reinvests coupons at a higher rate
An investor sells a bond back to the issuer under a put
An issuer sets money aside to repay bonds
w: Correct: this is the refinancing logic, similar to a homeowner refinancing a mortgage.
Wrong: reinvesting coupons has nothing to do with the issuer calling bonds.
Wrong: a put is an investor right, and refunding is an issuer action.
Wrong: that describes a sinking fund, which sets money aside for retirement, and not refunding, which replaces old debt with cheaper debt.

questions.q: A $1,000 par bond with a 5.5% coupon is called on a coupon date at a call price of 104. What does the holder receive in total, assuming par, final semiannual coupon and call premium are all paid?
w: Wrong: this omits the final semiannual coupon of $27.50 that is paid along with par and the premium on a call.
Correct: par $1,000 + final semiannual coupon $27.50 + call premium $40 = $1,067.50.
Wrong: this uses a full annual coupon of $55; only the final semiannual coupon of $27.50 is added.
Wrong: this leaves out the $40 call premium that a call price of 104 implies.

questions.q: A 25-year corporate bond is callable beginning in year 12. An investor asks when the issuer may redeem it. Which answer is accurate?
o: Only on a date the investor selects
At any time from year 12 until maturity, at the stated call price
w: Wrong: the call date marks when the right begins; it does not limit the call to that single year.
Wrong: redemption at maturity is not a call; the call right exists before maturity.
Wrong: a call is the issuer’s option, so the investor does not choose the date.
Correct: a callable bond is usually callable at any time after the call date.

questions.q: Compared with an otherwise identical straight bond, how will a callable bond and a puttable bond generally be priced for yield?
o: Callable pays a higher rate; puttable pays a lower rate
Callable pays a lower rate; puttable pays a higher rate
w: Correct: the call benefits the issuer so investors demand more, while the put benefits investors so they accept less.
Wrong: this reverses which party benefits from each feature, so the pricing consequence is backwards for both bonds.
Wrong: a put protects the investor, so it lowers the required yield rather than raising it.
Wrong: a call hurts the investor, so callable bonds must pay more, not less.

questions.q: An investor wants the right to sell a bond back to the issuer if its credit rating drops. Which feature does she need?
w: Wrong: a call gives the issuer, not the investor, the redemption right.
Wrong: a sinking fund sets money aside for retirement and gives no right to demand repayment.
Correct: a put lets the investor demand early repayment on a trigger such as a rating downgrade.
Wrong: a floating coupon changes the interest rate and does not give a redemption right.

questions.q:
Which of the following would the holder of a called 6% bond (callable at 102) receive on the call date?
I. Par value
II. Final semiannual coupon
III. A call premium
IV. Further interest for the next six months
w: Wrong: a call price of 102 means the call premium of $20 is also paid.
Correct: par, the last semiannual coupon, and the $20 premium are paid; interest stops after the call.
Wrong: par is also returned, and interest does not continue after a call.
Wrong: interest ceases once the bond is called, so IV is false.

questions.q: A corporate bond pays $27.50 of interest every six months. What is its nominal yield?
w: Wrong: this uses the semiannual payment alone; the yield is based on annual interest.
Wrong: this doubles the annual amount; $27.50 twice is $55, not $110.
Wrong: $55 of annual interest divided by $1,000 of par is 5.5%, not 5.0%, so the arithmetic is off.

questions.q: A 6% bond is trading at 80. What is its current yield?
w: Wrong: that is the nominal yield; current yield uses the market price of $800.
Correct: annual interest of $60 divided by the market price of $800 gives a current yield of 7.5%.
Wrong: this divides $60 by $1,250, which is not the market price; a quote of 80 means $800.
Wrong: $60 divided by $800 is exactly 7.5%, so 8.0% results from an arithmetic or rounding error.

questions.q: A bond pays $22.50 every six months and is quoted at 90. What is its current yield?
w: Correct: annual interest = $22.50 × 2 = $45; $45 ÷ $900 = 5.0%.
Wrong: this fails to annualize the coupon: $22.50 ÷ $900 is only 2.5%.
Wrong: this divides $45 by par of $1,000 and gives the nominal yield, not current yield.
Wrong: this halves the coupon and divides by par, doubling the mistake.

questions.q: Years ago an investor bought a 7% bond at 110. The bond now trades at 98. What is the current yield, rounded to two decimals?
w: Wrong: this divides $70 by the $1,100 purchase price; current yield uses today’s market price.
Wrong: that is the nominal yield and ignores the current market price.
Correct: annual interest of $70 divided by today’s market price of $980 gives 7.14%, ignoring the old purchase price.
Wrong: this divides $70 by $910, but the bond’s current market price is $980 (a quote of 98).

questions.q: A bond is trading at a premium. Which of the following is TRUE?
o: Its current yield is higher than its nominal yield
Its current yield is lower than its nominal yield
Its yield to call is higher than its yield to maturity
Its nominal yield is lower than its yield to maturity
w: Wrong: for a premium bond the price is above par so current yield is below nominal yield.
Correct: a price above par makes annual interest ÷ price smaller than the coupon rate.
Wrong: for a premium bond the premium is lost faster at call, so YTC is lower than YTM.
Wrong: for a premium bond YTM is below the coupon, so nominal yield is higher.

questions.q: A 6% bond with 12 years to maturity is trading at 106 and is callable in three years at 102. Which of the following lists its yields from highest to lowest?
o: Nominal yield, current yield, yield to maturity, yield to call
Yield to call, yield to maturity, current yield, nominal yield
Current yield, nominal yield, yield to maturity, yield to call
Nominal yield, yield to maturity, current yield, yield to call
w: Correct: for a premium bond NY > CY > YTM > YTC, so yield to call is lowest.
Wrong: this is the discount-bond ordering and is reversed for a premium.
Wrong: nominal yield is above current yield for a premium bond, so these two are swapped.
Wrong: current yield sits above yield to maturity for a premium bond, so these are swapped.

questions.q: A 7% bond is described as trading on an 8 basis. Which statement is correct?
o: It is trading at a discount
It is trading at a premium
The price cannot be determined without the maturity date
w: Correct: a yield to maturity of 8% above the 7% coupon means the bond was bought below par.
Wrong: a premium bond would have a YTM below its coupon, not above.
Wrong: at par the yield to maturity equals the coupon, but this bond trades above par, so that does not apply.
Wrong: the relationship between YTM and coupon alone tells you whether it is a discount.

questions.q: A bond has three possible future call dates. Which date is used to compute its yield to call?
o: The average of the three dates
w: Correct: YTC always uses the first possible call date and any call premium payable then.
Wrong: the last date is not used; yield to call assumes the earliest redemption.
Wrong: averaging the possible dates is not part of the calculation, which always uses the first possible call date.
Wrong: using the maturity date would give yield to maturity, not yield to call.

questions.q: Which type of bond has no reinvestment risk?
o: A 10-year municipal bond with semiannual coupons
w: Wrong: a callable bond pays coupons and may be redeemed early, so reinvestment risk is real.
Wrong: a municipal bond with semiannual coupons pays interest that must be reinvested, so reinvestment risk is present.
Wrong: floating notes pay periodic interest that has to be reinvested, so they still carry reinvestment risk.
Correct: because a zero-coupon bond pays no coupons, there is no periodic interest to reinvest at a lower rate.

questions.q: Interest rates are expected to fall. Which bond would appreciate the most?
w: Wrong: short maturity and a high coupon make it the least rate-sensitive of these.
Wrong: a zero is sensitive but its short maturity limits the price move.
Wrong: long maturity helps, but the high coupon reduces sensitivity compared with a zero.
Correct: long maturity and no coupon give the longest duration, so the largest price gain.

questions.q:
Which of the following would INCREASE a bond’s sensitivity to interest rate changes?
I. A longer maturity
II. A lower coupon
III. A longer duration
IV. A shorter maturity
w: Wrong: longer duration also reflects greater sensitivity, so III belongs in the answer.
Wrong: a shorter maturity decreases rate sensitivity, so statement IV is false and cannot be part of the answer.
Correct: longer maturity, lower coupon and longer duration all raise interest rate sensitivity.
Wrong: a shorter maturity reduces interest rate risk, so IV is false and selecting every statement is incorrect.

questions.q: An investor owns a long-term 7% bond. The Fed announces rate cuts and the investor worries that the $70 received each year can only be reinvested at lower rates. This concern is:
w: Wrong: credit risk concerns the issuer’s ability to pay, which is not at issue here.
Correct: the risk is that interest received must be reinvested at lower rates than the bond paid.
Wrong: inflationary risk is loss of purchasing power, not lower reinvestment rates.
Wrong: the concern is about the rate earned on proceeds, not the ability to sell.

questions.q: Call risk most directly leads to which other risk for the investor?
o: Interest rate risk on a zero-coupon bond
w: Correct: after a call in a low-rate world, the investor cannot find a similar return.
Wrong: a call is the issuer exercising a right and is not a sign of default.
Wrong: a call does not affect purchasing power directly; inflationary risk comes from rising consumer prices, not redemption.
Wrong: a call does not create a zero-coupon exposure, and interest rate risk on zeros is a separate concept.

questions.q: Inflation in an economy rises sharply and the Federal Reserve responds by raising interest rates. What is the combined effect on holders of long-term fixed-rate bonds?
o: Their purchasing power rises and bond prices rise
Their coupon buys fewer goods and bond prices fall
Their coupon buys fewer goods but bond prices rise
Their purchasing power is unchanged and bond prices fall
w: Wrong: inflation erodes purchasing power rather than raising it, and higher rates push bond prices down, not up.
Correct: fixed interest loses purchasing power and higher rates push bond prices down.
Wrong: the second half is wrong because higher interest rates cause bond prices to fall rather than rise.
Wrong: fixed payments lose purchasing power during inflation, so purchasing power cannot be unchanged for these holders.

questions.q: Which statement about US government securities is NOT correct?
o: They are considered free of credit risk because the government can tax
They are still exposed to inflationary risk
They carry lower yields than comparable corporate bonds
They have no interest rate risk
w: Wrong: this is true and is the source of the risk-free credit label.
Wrong: this is a true statement, since fixed payments lose purchasing power, so it cannot be the exception.
Wrong: lowest default risk goes with the lowest return, so this is true.
Correct: this is false because their prices fall when interest rates rise.

questions.q: Which Moody’s rating is the lowest investment grade?
w: Wrong: this is the first non-investment-grade rating, one notch below investment grade.
Correct: Baa3 corresponds to BBB− on the S&P and Fitch scale and is the lowest investment-grade rating.
Wrong: A3 is investment grade but sits several notches above the lowest investment-grade level of Baa3.
Wrong: Caa1 is deep in non-investment-grade territory, far below the investment-grade cutoff at Baa3.

questions.q: Which of the following is considered a non-investment-grade (junk) rating?
w: Wrong: BBB− is the lowest investment-grade rating on the S&P and Fitch scale.
Wrong: Baa2 is a mid-level investment-grade Moody’s rating, which sits above the junk cutoff at Ba1.
Correct: BB+ is the first rung below investment grade, so the bond is junk.
Wrong: A− is an investment-grade rating well above the cutoff, so the bond is not junk.

questions.q:
Which of the following are TRUE of non-investment-grade bonds?
I. They carry a higher chance of default
II. They pay higher yields
III. They are also called high-yield bonds
IV. They pay lower yields than investment-grade bonds
w: Correct: junk bonds carry more credit risk, pay more, and are known as high-yield bonds.
Wrong: IV is false and II and III are true, so this misses two correct statements.
Wrong: II is true but IV contradicts it, and I and III are also true.
Wrong: IV is false because junk bonds must pay more, not less.

questions.q: The Electronic Municipal Market Access (EMMA) website is operated by which organization?
w: Wrong: FINRA regulates broker-dealers and their registered people but does not operate the EMMA municipal website.
Wrong: the SEC is the federal regulator and not the operator of EMMA.
Correct: EMMA is a public online resource run by the Municipal Securities Rulemaking Board.
Wrong: the Federal Reserve has no role in operating EMMA, which is run by the MSRB for municipal securities.

questions.q: A customer buys a 6% corporate bond that pays interest on January 1 and July 1. The trade is on March 10 and settles the next business day, March 11. How much accrued interest does the buyer owe per $1,000 bond?
w: Wrong: this uses 60 days; the count must run from January 1 through March 10, which is 70 days.
Wrong: this counts 68 days; the days from January 1 through March 10 total 70.
Wrong: this counts 72 days, which wrongly includes the settlement date and an extra day.

questions.q: A 3% Treasury note pays interest on May 15 and November 15. The investor buys on August 12 for regular-way settlement on August 13. Accrued interest runs from May 15 to August 12 inclusive, which is 90 days. What accrued interest is due per $1,000 note?
w: Correct: Treasuries use actual days and a 365-day year: $30 × 90 ÷ 365 = $7.40.
Wrong: this applies the 360-day year used for corporate, municipal and agency bonds.
Wrong: this uses 89 days, dropping a day that should be counted.
Wrong: this uses 91 days, which wrongly includes the settlement date in the count of accrued days.

questions.q: A customer buys three corporate bonds quoted at 101 1/2 in the secondary market. Accrued interest is $9.00 per bond. What is the total amount due at settlement, ignoring commissions?
w: Correct: each bond is $1,015 + $9 accrued = $1,024, and 3 × $1,024 = $3,072.
Wrong: this omits accrued interest, which the buyer pays on top of the price.
Wrong: this adds the $9 of accrued interest only once rather than for each of the three bonds.
Wrong: this treats 1/2 as 0.25, giving $1,025 per bond, so the price is overstated.

questions.q:
Which of the following bonds trade flat?
I. A zero-coupon bond
II. A bond in default
III. A 5% corporate bond sold between coupon dates
IV. A Treasury note sold between coupon dates
w: Wrong: a bond in default also trades flat, so selecting only the zero-coupon bond leaves out a correct item.
Correct: zero-coupon bonds and bonds in default trade flat, with no accrued interest added to the price.
Wrong: bonds sold between coupon dates trade with accrued interest, so III is wrong.
Wrong: these are bonds that trade with accrued interest, the opposite of flat, so III and IV do not qualify.

questions.q: Which pairing of bond type and accrued-interest day count is correct?
w: Wrong: Treasuries use actual days and a 365-day year, not the 360-day convention shown in this option.
Wrong: corporate bonds use a 360-day year with 30-day months, not a 365-day actual-day count.
Wrong: municipal bonds follow the same 360-day, 30-day-month convention as corporates, not actual days.
Correct: corporate, municipal and agency bonds all use a 360-day year with 30-day months.

questions.q: A customer buys a corporate bond on a Friday for regular-way settlement. Up to which day is accrued interest counted?
o: Sunday, the day before the Monday settlement
w: Wrong: trade date plus settlement matters; interest runs to the day before settlement, which is later than Friday.
Wrong: interest continues over the weekend, so Saturday is counted, but so is Sunday.
Correct: T+1 from a Friday settles on Monday, and interest counts up to but not including settlement, so through Sunday.
Wrong: the settlement date itself is excluded from the count, so interest stops the day before settlement.

questions.q: A customer buys a bond between coupon dates. Who pays accrued interest and to whom?
w: Correct: accrued interest is added to the price so the seller receives the interest earned during his ownership.
Wrong: the seller is owed the interest, not the other way around.
Wrong: the issuer’s coupon is paid on the coupon date and is unrelated to the trade payment.
Wrong: the payment goes between buyer and seller, not to the issuer.

questions.q: A seller receives accrued interest in a bond trade. How is this amount treated?
o: Capital gain that increases cost basis
Interest income that increases cost basis
Ordinary interest income that does not affect cost basis
w: Wrong: accrued interest is interest income taxed at ordinary rates, not a capital gain, and it leaves cost basis alone.
Wrong: accrued interest is taxable and is not a return of principal.
Wrong: accrued interest does not change the bond’s cost basis, so it cannot increase basis at all.
Correct: it is taxed at ordinary income rates and leaves cost basis unchanged.

questions.q: An investor buys a bond for $880 with eight years to maturity. Using straight-line accretion, what is her cost basis after three years?
w: Wrong: this adds only one year of accretion ($15) instead of three.
Correct: the discount of $120 ÷ 8 years = $15 a year; after three years $880 + $45 = $925.
Wrong: this subtracts the accretion, but a discount bond’s basis rises toward par.
Wrong: this uses four years of accretion at $15 a year rather than three, giving $940 instead of $925.

questions.q: An investor buys a bond for $1,120 with six years to maturity. Using straight-line amortization, what is her cost basis after four years?
w: Wrong: this adds to the basis, but a premium bond’s basis falls toward par.
Wrong: this uses one year of amortization of $20, not four years.
Correct: the premium of $120 ÷ 6 years = $20 a year; after four years $1,120 − $80 = $1,040.
Wrong: this subtracts only three years of amortization, $60, from $1,120 instead of the four years asked.

questions.q: A customer buys a bond at a premium. For tax purposes the cost basis must be:
o: left unchanged until the bond is sold
w: Wrong: accretion upward toward par applies to bonds bought at a discount, but this bond was bought at a premium.
Wrong: accrued interest does not change cost basis, so it plays no role in the premium adjustment.
Wrong: the IRS requires an annual straight-line adjustment toward par, so leaving the basis unchanged is incorrect.
Correct: premium bonds are amortized on a straight-line basis so that the basis equals par at maturity.

questions.q: A customer expects interest rates to climb and wants the bond type that is least likely to lose market value as a result. Which choice best fits?
o: A floating-rate bond tied to the Treasury bill rate
w: Wrong: this has the greatest price sensitivity and would be hurt the most.
Correct: the coupon adjusts with the benchmark, so it has little or no interest rate risk.
Wrong: a long maturity with a low coupon is highly rate-sensitive, so it would lose value if rates climb.
Wrong: a fixed coupon still loses market value when rates rise, because new bonds would offer better rates.

questions.q: A corporate issuer misses a scheduled interest payment on an outstanding bond. What is the result?
o: The bond is automatically called at par
w: Wrong: a missed payment is not a call, which is the issuer’s option.
Wrong: a missed payment does not extend the maturity date; it simply means the issuer has defaulted on its obligation.
Correct: a missed interest payment on an outstanding obligation is a default; credit risk has materialized.
Wrong: there is no automatic increase in the coupon after a missed payment.
